newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. urges renewal of stalled Sahara operation.
newsitem.headline: U.N. urges renewal of stalled Sahara operation.

text.p: Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali recommended on Thursday a six-month renewal of the U.N. operation in Western Sahara despite continuing deadlock over plans for a referendum on whether the territory should be incorporated into Morocco or become independent.
In a report to the Security Council, he referred to "recent indications that the parties are moving forward" and urged that more time be allowed "for further progress."

The referendum was to have been held in January 1992. But Morocco, which controls most of the former Spanish colony, and the Polisario Front, which has been battling for independence, disagree on who should be eligible to vote. Voter identification was halted nearly a year ago.

Boutros-Ghali said that, in accordance with a May Security Council resolution, the U.N. Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara (MINURSO) had been reduced from a strength of 288 military observers to 230 and from 91 police to nine, while civilian staff had been cut from 410 to 170.
His optimism about "moving forward" appeared to be based on recent reports of the first private meetings for several years between representatives of Morocco and Polisario.

Alluding to those encounters, he wrote: "It is encouraging that on Oct. 10, 1996, the Fourth Committee of the General Assembly was informed that contacts had taken place, would continue to take place and that those contacts would certainly not lose sight of the (U.N.) settlement plan which governs the holding of the referendum."
Morocco's King Hassan said on Wednesday talks had been held recently in Morocco with Polisario but had been inconclusive.

"We agreed to meet them but on condition that the question of independence was not on the table. Our son (Crown Prince Sidi Mohammed) and the Interior Minister (Driss Basri) held talks with them during two days," the king said, adding: "The talks ended (but) not on the basis of a breakdown. We agreed to leave the door open when matters have matured."

Boutros-Ghali said in his report Morocco and Polisario had "reiterated their commitment to the settlement plan," continued to respect a ceasefire which has largely held since September 1991, and were hopeful that ways might be found to permit the resumption of voter identification.

He urged the parties to continue cooperating with his acting special representative for the Western Sahara, Erik Jensen, in his efforts to resolve the outstanding questions concerning the U.N. settlement plan.

"In view of the recent indications that the parties are moving forward in this direction, and in order to allow time for further progress, I recommend that the Security Counciul extend MINURSO's mandate for a further period of six months until May 31, 1997," he said.

But, reflecting growing impatience, he said the international community "cannot be expected to support the extension of the mandate of MINURSO indefinitely unless there is tangible progress towards the settlement of the question of Western Sahara."

The secretary-general said that, while the ceasefire continued to hold, there had been "some technical violations of it, as well as an intensification of military activity on both sides, apparently aimed at ensuring combat readiness as the end of MINURSO's current mandate period approaches."
